## About Dynamic Risk Prediction

Traditional risk prediction generates a risk estimate at a defined timepoint in a patient’s disease trajectory, for example the risk of death within 30 days following a surgical procedure. In contrast, dynamic risk prediction enables prediction of risk at any time point. Risk prediction helps detect disease early, prevent illness, and target treatments efficiently.
Predictive analytics enables proactive care by identifying at-risk patients before symptoms worsen, allowing earlier intervention when treatments are most effective.
Risk is dynamic, not static. It changes with disease duration and patient health status. Traditional single-snapshot models fail to capture this evolution.
Dynamic prediction models are effective because it can:

- Detect diseases on early stages
- Prevent development of the diseases
- Provide the appropriate treatment
- Help allocate resources efficiently


These tools support clinicians' decision-making, and they allows to continuously monitor a patient’s risk which forms the basis for intervention if the predicted risk increases. In this course, we will explore methodological and technical solutions, as well as corresponding challenges, for developing and implementing such solutions in health care.

In the following figure you see an illustration of the complex decision-making process clinicians navigate during patient interactions, with a focus on the critical questions they must address and how these considerations evolve throughout the patient's care timeline.

In detail, the course includes the following topics::

- 1) Data management: This part of the course considers the challenges of preparing heterogenous longitudinal health data for prediction. We will cover the various steps involved in this process, including data formatting, feature engineering, and splitting strategies for model validation. This will include discussion about how to handle irregularly sampled health data, data leakage, class imbalance, temporal robustness, normalization, and other potential biases.

- 2) Modelling: In this part of the course, participants will be led through the process of building such models. We will introduce both basic and more advanced dynamic machine learning prediction algorithms, such as gradient tree boosting, random forest, and LSTM and discuss issues related to performance metrics and hyperparameter optimization, for example Bayesian optimization.

- 3) Implementation: In the last part of the course, we will consider the challenges associated with the implementation of predictive tools in the clinic. This includes technical aspects about hosting, user interface, and access to live data, including an introduction to the FHIR standard. Regulatory and organizational issues will also be discussed. During the project the participants will get hands on experience covering realistic scenarios related to the subjects discussed. This will include data management of representative data sets, training models and hands on introduction to the FHIR set-up.



## What do we need to setup dynamic risk

To set-up dynamic risk prediction, we introduce the following notation:

- Cohort of patients: A group of individuals being monitored over time for clinical outcomes or disease progression.
- Prediction time points $t_{ij}$ for the patient $i'th$ and $j'th$ time point: The specific moments when predictions are made.
- Binary outcome $Y(t_{ij})$ for each prediction time: clinical outcome measures as "yes/no" (like disease, hospitalization, or recovery, etc) at each prediction time point.
- Baseline/static data $X_i$ for the patient $i'th$: These are characteristics that do not change over time for each patient, such as biological sex, date of birth, or genetic factors.
- Time dependent data $Z_i(t)$ for patient $i$: These are measurements that change over time, like weight, lab values, or prescriptions of medicine and amount collected at various time points.
- The time when predictive data is collected at time point $t$ may differ from the prediction time points ($t_{ij}$), reflecting real-world clinical practice where measurements are not always synchronized with prediction needs.

## Motivational example
Administration of Systemic Anti-Cancer Treatment (SACT) is a motivation for prediction systems for cancer patients, as ensuring patients receive the right SACT at the right time will not only optimize survival rates, but also potentially maximize the quality of remaining life for patients. There is a fine balance regarding when to provide a patient SACT as it can decrease a patient's quality of life over time. The purpose of SACT is to provide the highest degree of life quality for a patient in palliative treatment (best-case scenario). However, it can cause a patient to suffer more in their remaining lifetime, which could mean that a patient's outcome would be worse with SACT than without (worst-case scenario). Therefore, dynamic predictive models are an important measure to help clinicians make better informed decisions to either save the patient or to spare them suffering.

**A model of health-related quality of life for a patient with limited survival:** A illustration of the possible scenarious in short-term survial predictions. The illustratin stems from [Vesteghem, 2022](https://vbn.aau.dk/ws/portalfiles/portal/549539126/phd_CPEV_e_pdf.pdf)[^1]

## Health Data for Prediction Models

Prediction models need large amounts of high-quality, sequential data to recognize patterns and make accurate forecasts based on past trends.
Data collection involves multiple stakeholders and requires access to restricted health databases like PAS (Patient Administration System), MedOnc (Medical Oncology), LABKA (Lab Information System), and Patobank (Pathology Registry). These sources provide important patient information for accurate predictions.
After securing database access, relevant variables must be identified and combined into a unified framework for analysis. Time factors are critical variables for prediction models. For example, predicting 30-day mortality requires specific temporal markers such as diagnosis date, palliative treatment initiation, and time of death, among other relevant markers.

**Example of records for a patient:** This figure shows patient survival predictions made at various time points, where each dot represents a data point, with markers for clinical factors including ALK, anaplastic lymphoma kinase gene, BMI, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, C-reactive protein, lactate dehydrogenase, treatment. The figure stems from [Vesteghem, et al., 2022](https://ascopubs.org/doi/pdfdirect/10.1200/CCI.22.00054)[^2].

# Summary

In this introduction, an overview was provided on how to access all the resources of this course.
The structure for the entire course was presented, including all segments and their content.
There was a brief introduction to the concept of dynamic risk prediction and how it differs from traditional risk prediction in healthcare.
A high-level overview of the implementation of such a system was provided, where the main topics were introduced:

- Data management
- Modelling
- Implementation

A setup for dynamic risk assessment was presented along with an overview of the necessary materials to build dynamic risk models.
A short description of the reasoning behind risk and dynamic models was provided.
